lesson.title: Four Corners of a Pyramid: The Tetrahedral Shape
lesson.summary: Tetrahedral geometry spreads four electron domains into three dimensions at 109.5 degree angles, the single most common shape in organic chemistry and the geometry behind methane's perfect symmetry.
lesson.body:
Tetrahedral geometry is what appears once a central atom has four electron domains with no lone pairs among them. Unlike linear and trigonal planar geometry, which can both be drawn flat on a page, four repelling regions cannot all reach their maximum possible separation while staying in a single plane. The domains have to escape into three dimensions, spreading out toward the four corners of a shape called a tetrahedron, a pyramid built from four triangular faces. The bond angle that results from this arrangement is 109.5 degrees between every pair of adjacent domains, and because there are no lone pairs here to set aside, the electron geometry and molecular geometry are once again the same shape, both called tetrahedral.

Methane, CH4, is the defining example of tetrahedral geometry. Carbon sits at the center with four single bonds to four hydrogen atoms and no lone pairs remaining, since carbon's four valence electrons are entirely used up in those four bonds. With a steric number of four and zero lone pairs, methane adopts an ideal tetrahedral shape, and because all four substituents are identical hydrogen atoms, every H to C to H angle measures exactly 109.5 degrees. All four C to H bonds are completely equivalent by symmetry, which is part of why methane is such a stable, nonpolar, and chemically unremarkable molecule under normal conditions.

Tetrahedral geometry is, without much competition, the most important shape in organic chemistry. Nearly every carbon atom that forms four single bonds, whether in a simple chain, a branched structure, or a large biological molecule, adopts this same tetrahedral arrangement around itself. This is why carbon backbones in organic molecules zigzag through space rather than lying in a straight line: each carbon's four bonds point toward the corners of its own local tetrahedron, and stringing many of these tetrahedral centers together naturally produces the zigzag, three dimensional skeletons seen in everything from simple alkanes to complex natural products.

It is worth connecting tetrahedral geometry directly back to electron geometry to avoid a common source of confusion. A central atom can have a tetrahedral electron geometry, meaning four total domains, without having a tetrahedral molecular geometry, if one or more of those domains is a lone pair rather than a bonding pair. Methane, with zero lone pairs, keeps the full tetrahedral molecular shape. But swapping one bonding pair for a lone pair, while keeping the same steric number of four, produces trigonal pyramidal geometry instead, and swapping two bonding pairs for lone pairs produces bent geometry, both covered in later chapters.

This progression, tetrahedral electron geometry giving rise to three different molecular geometries depending on how many of the four domains are lone pairs, is one of the clearest demonstrations of how VSEPR theory really works. The underlying electron arrangement stays constant at a steric number of four, spread out 109.5 degrees apart in principle, but the visible shape traced out by the atoms alone changes dramatically depending on how many of those four positions are actually occupied by a bonded atom versus a lone pair sitting quietly out of view.
